question: The Norse myths describe the signs of Ragnarok beginning long before the final battle. Three winters of unbroken cold came one after another with no summer between them, the sun grown weak and the snow never melting. Brother slew brother for food and warmth, kinsmen drowned each other in the rivers, and morality collapsed. Wolves swallowed the sun and moon. The cock Gullinkambi crowed in Valhalla to wake the slain warriors for the last battle, while a sooty-red rooster crowed in Hel for the dead there. What was the name of this three-winter signal?
answer: Fimbulwinter
choices: Fimbulwinter
Gimlewinter
Hodrwinter
Niflwinter
context: Fimbulwinter is described in the Voluspa and the Prose Edda. Snorri Sturluson wrote that brothers would 'stain one another with blood' and that 'an axe-age, a sword-age, shields shall be cloven' would precede the world's end. Some scholars connect the imagery to the climate disasters following the 536 AD volcanic dust veil that darkened skies across northern Europe.

question: Heimdall was the watchman of the gods, standing eternally at the post Himinbjorg where the rainbow bridge Bifrost touched Asgard. He could hear grass growing on the earth and wool growing on the backs of sheep, see for a hundred leagues by day or night, and needed less sleep than a bird. He kept a great horn ready to sound when the giants finally marched on Asgard at Ragnarok. When the first signs began, Heimdall lifted the horn to his lips and blew a single blast so loud it echoed through all nine worlds and woke the Aesir to arm themselves. What was the name of Heimdall's horn?
answer: Gjallarhorn
choices: Gjallarhorn
Olifant
Brimir
Vingnir
context: The Gjallarhorn appears in both the Poetic Edda and Snorri's Prose Edda. The name means roughly 'resounding horn' or 'yelling horn.' Heimdall was said to be the son of nine mothers and the brightest of the gods. He and Loki had been enemies from the start and were destined to kill each other at Ragnarok.

question: Fenrir the wolf, son of Loki, had been bound on the lonely island of Lyngvi with the magical fetter Gleipnir, made by the dwarfs from six impossible things. The gods had bound him only by the trick of the war-god Tyr placing his right hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge of good faith — and Fenrir bit it off when he realized the trick. There Fenrir had waited and grown for ages, mouth propped open with a sword, a river of saliva called Von flowing from his jaws. At the first signal of Ragnarok the fetter snapped. The wolf shook himself free and ran for the field of Vigrid where the gods awaited. What did Fenrir's open jaws span from earth to heaven as he ran?
answer: His upper jaw scraped the sky while the lower dragged the ground
choices: His upper jaw scraped the sky while the lower dragged the ground
Fire poured from his mouth setting forests blazing for leagues
His breath froze every river solid for nine days afterward
Eight of his teeth fell out and grew into new wolves
context: The image is from the Voluspa: 'gaping mouth, the lower jaw rests on the earth, the upper reaches heaven.' Fenrir was destined to swallow Odin himself. The river Von, which flowed from his jaws during his binding, was named for the Old Norse word for 'hope' — bitter irony for the gods who had bound him.

question: Jormungandr, the world serpent, was Loki's second monstrous child. Odin had thrown the young serpent into the ocean encircling Midgard, where it grew so vast it could bite its own tail around the whole world. Thor and Jormungandr had clashed twice before Ragnarok: once when Thor tried to lift a giant cat that was the serpent in disguise (he raised one paw), and once when Thor hooked Jormungandr while fishing with the giant Hymir (the giant cut the line in terror). At Ragnarok the serpent finally released its tail and rose. What did Jormungandr do to the sea and the land as it came onto shore?
answer: Flooded the land with venom poured from its open mouth
choices: Flooded the land with venom poured from its open mouth
Drank the entire ocean dry in a single swallow
Coiled itself around Asgard and squeezed the walls flat
Turned to stone and blocked every harbor in Midgard
context: Snorri's Prose Edda describes the serpent 'blowing so much venom that he bespatters all the air and sea.' The two would meet for their fated third encounter on the field of Vigrid. Jormungandr's name means roughly 'huge monster' or 'great beast.' He was also called the Midgard Serpent.

question: On the field of Vigrid at Ragnarok, Thor and Jormungandr finally met for the third and final time. The thunder god, wearing his iron gauntlets Jarngreipr and his strength-doubling belt Megingjord, swung Mjolnir at the world serpent. The hammer struck home and crushed Jormungandr's skull. The serpent was killed. But Thor had been splashed with venom in the fight, and the poison had reached his lungs. He did not fall immediately. The Voluspa says he managed a specific number of paces back from the dead serpent before the venom dropped him. How many steps did Thor stagger before dying?
answer: Nine
choices: Nine
Three
Twelve
Seven
context: Both the Voluspa and Snorri's Prose Edda give the same count of nine. The number nine recurs throughout Norse mythology: nine worlds on Yggdrasil, nine nights Odin hung from the tree for the runes, nine mothers of Heimdall, nine daughters of the sea-god Aegir. Thor was the most beloved of the Aesir to ordinary farmers, and amulets of Mjolnir survive from across Viking-age Scandinavia.

question: At Ragnarok on the field of Vigrid, Odin rode out at the head of the Einherjar — the slain heroes from Valhalla — wearing his golden helmet and carrying his spear Gungnir. He rode straight for Fenrir, his fated enemy. The two clashed. Odin's spear could pierce any armor and Gungnir's point had been the witness to oaths in the nine worlds. But Fenrir was the vast wolf whose jaws stretched from earth to heaven. What happened to the All-Father in the duel?
answer: Fenrir swallowed Odin whole in one bite
choices: Fenrir swallowed Odin whole in one bite
Odin drove Gungnir through the wolf's throat
The two fought to exhaustion and parted for a final round
Odin transformed into an eagle and escaped at the last moment
context: Odin's fate had been known to him for ages — the Norns had spoken of it and the volva (seeress) had told him in the Voluspa. Knowing his end did not change his choice to ride out. Odin's hall Valhalla had been built specifically to gather warriors for this battle: the Einherjar feasted and fought every day in preparation. The All-Father died first among the major gods.

question: Vidar was Odin's silent son by the giantess Grid. He had been preparing for one purpose since the beginning: avenging his father at Ragnarok. The Norse had a custom of throwing away the leather scraps trimmed from shoe-tops and heels. For ages Vidar had gathered every such scrap from every shoemaker in the nine worlds and used them to build a single enormous boot, reinforced with iron, fit only for his right foot. When Fenrir swallowed Odin, Vidar stepped forward and pressed that boot into the wolf's lower jaw, anchoring it to the ground. What did he do with his hands?
answer: Gripped the upper jaw and tore Fenrir apart from the inside
choices: Gripped the upper jaw and tore Fenrir apart from the inside
Stabbed Gungnir down through the wolf's open throat
Pulled out the wolf's heart still beating for sacrifice
Shouted three words of binding that froze the beast in place
context: Vidar was called 'the Silent God' and was almost never named in stories before this moment. Some scholars believe his cult prepared sacred shoes specifically associated with revenge oaths. The boot motif is rare in mythology and uniquely Norse. Vidar was one of the few gods who would survive Ragnarok and walk in the renewed world.

question: Loki and Heimdall had been enemies from the start. Heimdall the watchman saw everything; Loki the trickster betrayed everything. When Loki helped Hodr kill Balder, the gods finally caught Loki and bound him with the entrails of his own son Vali (transformed into a wolf) to three sharp stones in a cavern. The goddess Skadi hung a serpent dripping venom over his face. His wife Sigyn caught the venom in a bowl, but each time she emptied the bowl, drops fell on Loki and his writhing caused earthquakes. At Ragnarok he broke free. On the field of Vigrid he and Heimdall met. What happened between them?
answer: They killed each other with mutual blows
choices: They killed each other with mutual blows
Loki fled into the rising tide and Heimdall followed alone
Heimdall split Loki in two with a single stroke and walked away
Loki tricked Heimdall into the wolf Fenrir's open jaws
context: The mutual-kill motif appears throughout Ragnarok: Thor and Jormungandr, Tyr and the hound Garm, Loki and Heimdall, Freyr and Surt (almost). The Norse vision of the end was a wave of paired destructions where each god and his fated enemy died together. Snorri's Prose Edda preserves most of these details from the older Voluspa.

question: Tyr was the bravest of the Aesir, the war-god who had placed his right hand in Fenrir's mouth as a pledge of good faith so the gods could bind the wolf with Gleipnir. When the wolf realized the binding would hold, he bit off Tyr's hand at the wrist — and the gods laughed except for Tyr. At Ragnarok the one-handed Tyr rode out to meet the great hound that guarded the gate of Hel. The hound's breast was always bloody from the gore of those who tried to pass it. Tyr and the hound met in single combat. What was the hound's name, and how did the fight end?
answer: Garm — they killed each other with mutual blows
choices: Garm — they killed each other with mutual blows
Sirius — Tyr cut off its head with a single stroke
Cerberus — it fled before the war-god's approach
Skoll — Tyr ripped out its throat with his remaining hand
context: Garm guarded the gate of Hel and is sometimes confused with Fenrir in later sources. The Voluspa names him separately. Tyr was the original Germanic sky-father god, displaced by Odin in the Norse pantheon — his name survives in Tuesday (Tiw's day) just as Odin's survives in Wednesday and Thor's in Thursday. Greek 'Cerberus' is the wrong tradition's hellhound but a plausible distractor for the unwary.

question: Freyr was the god of fertility, sunshine, and good harvests, ruler of Alfheim, lord of the elves. He had been given as a young god a sword that could swing itself and fight on its own — the finest blade in the nine worlds. But Freyr fell in love with the giantess Gerd, and he sent his messenger Skirnir to bring her back to him. To win the giant-bride, Freyr gave Skirnir his magic self-fighting sword as the brideprice. At Ragnarok Freyr met the fire-giant Surt — the lord of Muspelheim, whose flaming sword was brighter than the sun. What weapon did Freyr fight Surt with?
answer: A stag's antler, having given his sword away for Gerd long ago
choices: A stag's antler, having given his sword away for Gerd long ago
His own bare hands, refusing any weapon at the last battle
A spear borrowed from his father Njord of the sea
His golden boar Gullinbursti, charging it against the flames
context: Freyr's lost sword is the great cosmic mistake of Norse myth — the most powerful weapon in the nine worlds, given away for a giantess, missed when the worlds were on fire. He died to Surt. The Skirnismal in the Poetic Edda preserves the seduction-by-Skirnir story; the Voluspa preserves the sword-loss consequence at Ragnarok. Snorri specifically lamented the lost sword in the Prose Edda.

question: From Muspelheim, the southern realm of fire that had existed since before the world began, the fire-giant Surt rode out at the end of Ragnarok carrying a flaming sword brighter than the sun itself. He had been waiting at the borders of Muspelheim since the beginning of time for this single moment. He crossed Bifrost the rainbow bridge and the bridge shattered behind him. He killed Freyr on the field. Then he raised his burning blade. What did he do with the sword that ended the world?
answer: Ignited Yggdrasil, burning all nine worlds together
choices: Ignited Yggdrasil, burning all nine worlds together
Cut the rainbow bridge Bifrost in two so none could escape
Hurled it like a comet through the sky to fall on Asgard's halls
Plunged it down through Midgard cracking the earth in half
context: Surt is the oldest figure in Norse cosmology, predating even Odin and the Aesir. His name means 'black' or 'swarthy.' Iceland's Surtsey volcanic island that rose from the sea in 1963 was named for him. The Voluspa describes the final fire: 'the sun grows dark, the earth sinks in the sea, the bright stars fall from the sky, steam rises, flame plays against heaven itself.'

question: The Norse imagined the end of the world as a doom but not a final ending. After Surt's fire burned all nine worlds and the earth sank into the sea, a new green earth rose from the waves. Balder returned from Hel. The surviving Aesir (Vidar, Vali, Modi, Magni, Hodr) gathered on the field of Ida. The sons of Thor inherited Mjolnir. Two human survivors had hidden inside an enormous tree called Hoddmimir's wood, eating only the morning dew, and emerged when the new earth was ready to be repopulated. What were the names of the two survivors?
answer: Lif and Lifthrasir
choices: Lif and Lifthrasir
Ask and Embla
Bor and Bestla
Buri and Borr
context: Lif means 'Life' and Lifthrasir means 'Life-Striver' or 'Stubborn-Life.' Ask and Embla were the FIRST humans (created from logs by Odin and his brothers); Lif and Lifthrasir are the SECOND, the survivors who repopulate the renewed world. The Norse cycle was not creation-and-destruction but creation-destruction-renewal. The Vafthrudnismal in the Poetic Edda preserves this final consolation.

question: Sigurd was the greatest hero of the Volsung line. His foster-father was the dwarf smith Regin. Regin reforged for him the broken sword Gram from the shards of his ancestor Sigmund's blade — so sharp that when Sigurd tested it on the river Rhine, a falling tuft of wool floating downstream was cut in half by the edge resting in the water. Regin sent Sigurd to kill the dragon Fafnir (Regin's own brother, transformed by greed for the cursed gold). Sigurd dug a pit on Fafnir's path to drink at the river, hid below, and stabbed upward into the dragon's heart. While roasting the dragon's heart afterward, he accidentally tasted the blood. What new power did he gain?
answer: He could understand the speech of birds
choices: He could understand the speech of birds
He became invulnerable to all weapons forever after
He gained the strength of ten dragon-slayers combined
He could shape-shift into a dragon himself at will
context: Two nuthatches warned Sigurd that Regin planned to murder him in his sleep for the hoard. Sigurd killed Regin first by cutting off his head. The cursed treasure — once stolen from Odin by the dwarf Andvari with a ring that doubled gold — would destroy everyone who held it. Sigurd took the hoard, the ring Andvaranaut, and rode away on his horse Grani.

question: After killing the dragon Fafnir, Sigurd rode his horse Grani up a mountain named Hindarfjall surrounded by a wall of flickering flames. He rode through the flames unharmed and found at the summit a sleeping warrior in full armor. He cut away the helmet and the chain mail with his sword Gram. The figure beneath was no man but a Valkyrie, sleeping under a curse laid by Odin himself. The All-Father had pricked her with the sleeping-thorn for disobeying him in a battle — granting victory to the wrong king. Sigurd's blade woke her. What was the Valkyrie's name?
answer: Brunhild
choices: Brunhild
Sigrun
Gudrun
Idunn
context: Brunhild had vowed she would only marry a man brave enough to ride through her wall of fire. Sigurd and Brunhild exchanged oaths of love at her mountain hall and Sigurd gave her the cursed ring Andvaranaut as a betrothal gift. The Volsunga Saga and parts of the Poetic Edda preserve the story. Wagner's Ring Cycle operas restructure these scenes into Siegfried and Brunhilde.

question: After leaving Brunhild on her mountain with vows of love, Sigurd rode south to the hall of King Gjuki, lord of the Niflungs (also called the Burgundians). Gjuki's queen was Grimhild, a sorceress who saw at once that Sigurd would be the greatest match for her daughter Gudrun — but Sigurd was already betrothed to Brunhild. Grimhild brewed a potion and gave it to Sigurd at the welcome feast. He drank it. What did the potion do to him?
answer: It made him forget Brunhild entirely
choices: It made him forget Brunhild entirely
It killed him within three days of the welcome feast
It transformed him into a wolf for nine nights
It made him sleep for a hundred years like Brunhild had
context: The forgetting-potion is the linchpin of the tragedy. Without it, Sigurd would have remembered his vows and ridden on. With it, he married Gudrun and lived in the Niflung hall as Gunnar's brother-in-law. Grimhild's sorcery would set in motion the death of the greatest hero of the Volsung line. The motif of memory-potions appears across Norse and Germanic legend.

question: After marrying Gudrun, Sigurd discovered that her brother King Gunnar wanted to marry Brunhild — without knowing Sigurd's prior vows to her. Gunnar rode to Hindarfjall but his horse refused to enter Brunhild's wall of flame. Even on Sigurd's borrowed horse Grani, he could not pass. So Sigurd and Gunnar used the magical art Grimhild had taught them: they switched shapes. Sigurd in Gunnar's form rode Grani through the flames a second time. He stayed three nights with Brunhild as 'Gunnar.' What did Sigurd place between himself and Brunhild each night on the bed?
answer: His drawn sword Gram, blade pointed at the ceiling
choices: His drawn sword Gram, blade pointed at the ceiling
A cloak of silver thread woven by the goddess Frigg
A wooden plank carved with binding runes by the dwarfs
An iron chain blessed by the smiths of Svartalfheim
context: The bare sword between them preserved his honor toward Gudrun and toward Brunhild's vow to Gunnar. He took the cursed ring Andvaranaut back from Brunhild as a token of the marriage. She married Gunnar believing he had crossed the flames. The deception would unravel terribly. Wagner's Gotterdammerung preserves this scene as Siegfried's betrayal of Brunhilde.

question: Brunhild and Gudrun (Sigurd's wife) fell into a famous quarrel one day, washing their hair at a river. They argued over whose husband was greater. Gudrun finally proved her case by showing Brunhild the cursed ring Andvaranaut, claiming Sigurd had given it to her as proof that HE was the man who had ridden through Brunhild's wall of flame, not Gunnar. The truth of the shape-switching trick became clear. Brunhild had been deceived into marrying the lesser man. What did Brunhild demand from her husband Gunnar?
answer: That Sigurd be killed for the deception
choices: That Sigurd be killed for the deception
That Gunnar divorce her and let her ride back to her mountain
That Gudrun be exiled from the Niflung lands forever
That Sigurd return Andvaranaut to her hand at once
context: Brunhild's wrath drove the rest of the tragedy. She told Gunnar that Sigurd had violated her honor during the three nights — a lie to manipulate her husband. Gunnar and his brother Hogni were torn: they had sworn oaths of brotherhood to Sigurd, mingling blood in the earth. To kill him would be oath-breaking. But to lose Brunhild was unbearable. They turned to a way around the oath.

question: Gunnar and his brother Hogni had sworn blood-oaths of brotherhood to Sigurd that prevented them from killing him directly. To get around the oath they used their younger half-brother Gutthorm, who had sworn no such oath because he had not been present at the swearing. They fed Gutthorm a magical meal made of wolf's flesh, serpent's flesh, and other dark ingredients to madden his courage. Gutthorm slipped into Sigurd's chamber at dawn while Sigurd slept beside Gudrun. He drove a sword through the sleeping hero. What did the dying Sigurd manage to do?
answer: Hurled his own sword Gram and cut Gutthorm in half
choices: Hurled his own sword Gram and cut Gutthorm in half
Spoke a curse that doomed every Niflung to a violent death
Crawled to Brunhild's hall and forgave her before dying
Transformed into an eagle and flew away wounded to die
context: The Volsunga Saga and the Brot af Sigurdarkvidu describe the scene. Sigurd died in Gudrun's arms, his blood soaking her braids. Brunhild laughed once, then went quiet. The Niflungs had broken every oath of hospitality and brotherhood. The cursed Rhinegold hoard had taken its first great victim. Some versions have Sigurd killed in the woods instead of the bed — the bed version is the older.

question: After Sigurd's death, his body was placed on a great funeral pyre. His horse Grani lay down beside the pyre and refused to move. Brunhild dressed herself in her finest gold and her byrnie of mail. She gathered eight slaves and gave them gold to die with her. She climbed onto the pyre carrying Sigurd's drawn sword Gram. What did she do at the pyre?
answer: Killed herself with Sigurd's sword Gram and burned beside him
choices: Killed herself with Sigurd's sword Gram and burned beside him
Burned Gudrun's hair off as a final curse on the Niflung line
Set the entire Niflung hall alight from the funeral flames
Cut her own hair and cast it into the river Rhine as offering
context: Brunhild prophesied the future of every Niflung as she died — Gunnar's death in the snake-pit, Gudrun's revenge, Atli's downfall. She asked that her body burn beside Sigurd's with a drawn sword between them as it had been in their three nights, separating them even in death. The Volsunga Saga preserves her death-prophecy almost as a Sibyl's vision.

question: After Sigurd's death, Gudrun was forced into marriage with King Atli (the Norse name for the historical Attila the Hun). Atli wanted the Niflung hoard and lured Gudrun's brothers Gunnar and Hogni to his court. He killed Hogni first and cut out his heart. He threw Gunnar into a snake-pit, where Gunnar played a harp with his toes to charm the serpents — but one adder bit his liver and he died. Gudrun took her revenge on Atli in the same hall that night. She killed their two young sons (her own children with Atli), made cups from their skulls, and at the feast served Atli the boys' roasted hearts. What else did she do that night?
answer: Set Atli's entire hall on fire after he passed out drunk
choices: Set Atli's entire hall on fire after he passed out drunk
Took Atli's eyes with a knife while he slept beside her
Fled to Greece carrying the Rhinegold treasure with her
Cast herself into the river Rhine the next morning
context: Gudrun stabbed Atli to death first in his bed, then burned the hall with all his men inside. The Volsunga Saga and the Atlakvida preserve the gruesome detail. Gudrun's revenge is the Norse mirror of Medea's: a mother killing her own children to destroy a husband who had killed her brothers. She drowned herself afterward — or in other versions survived to a third marriage and more tragedy.

question: The cursed treasure that destroyed Sigurd, Brunhild, the Niflungs, and Atli began with a single ring. Long before any of them lived, Odin and his brothers had been traveling with the trickster god Loki when Loki killed an otter for sport — not knowing it was the shape-shifted son of a sorcerer named Hreidmar. To pay the wergild, Loki was sent to catch the dwarf Andvari (in fish-form in his river) and demand his treasure as ransom. Andvari surrendered his hoard, but Loki noticed the dwarf hiding one last ring on his finger and forced him to give it up. As Loki took it, Andvari spoke a curse. What was the curse the dwarf laid on the ring?
answer: That it would destroy everyone who possessed it
choices: That it would destroy everyone who possessed it
That it would turn its bearer into a dragon within a year
That it would multiply every winter without ever shrinking
That it could be removed only by the bearer's own son
context: The ring was Andvaranaut — 'Andvari's gift.' Hreidmar's sons Fafnir and Regin killed their father for the gold. Fafnir then took the hoard and turned into a dragon. Regin eventually used Sigurd to kill Fafnir, only to be killed himself. The cursed ring destroyed Sigurd, Brunhild, Gunnar, Hogni, Gutthorm, Atli, Gudrun's children. Tolkien drew on this directly for the One Ring of Lord of the Rings.

question: Sigurd was the greatest hero of the Volsung line, the family descended from Odin himself. His father Sigmund had once been the only man able to draw a sword that Odin (in disguise as a one-eyed wanderer) had thrust deep into the trunk of an oak tree at the heart of King Volsung's hall — a sword that became the family heirloom for generations. The sword was eventually shattered in battle when Sigmund was fighting against impossible odds. Old Sigmund was killed; his pregnant wife Hjordis fled to safety, carrying the shards of the shattered sword. The unborn child was Sigurd. Whose sword was it that Sigurd later had reforged?
answer: Gram — his father Sigmund's broken blade
choices: Gram — his father Sigmund's broken blade
Tyrfing — the cursed elf-forged blade of his great-uncle
Hofud — Heimdall's golden sword loaned to the Volsungs
Mistilteinn — a sea-king's sword recovered from the deep
context: Sigmund had been the chosen hero of Odin's tree-sword for one generation. The blade broke when Odin appeared again on the battlefield to end Sigmund's life — the All-Father lent and the All-Father reclaimed. Regin reforged Gram for Sigurd in two stories: in one he cut an anvil in half with the new blade; in another he tested it on a floating tuft of wool. Wagner's Siegfried renames Gram as 'Nothung' but the story is the same.

question: After the war between the Aesir and the Vanir (the two families of Norse gods) ended in peace, both sides sealed the treaty in the oldest way of human ritual: they spat into a single vat. From the gathered spittle of every god in both pantheons, the Aesir shaped a living wise man — the wisest being in the nine worlds. He could answer any question asked of him. He wandered the worlds giving counsel to those who needed it. Two dwarfs, Fjalar and Galar, invited him to their hall on the pretext of asking a question, then murdered him for his blood. What was the wise man's name?
answer: Kvasir
choices: Kvasir
Mimir
Hoenir
Vafthrudnir
context: Snorri's Prose Edda preserves the story in the Skaldskaparmal. Kvasir's name may be related to a fermented drink (kvas, Slavic kvass). The treaty-by-spittle is an ancient ritual that appears across many cultures. The wise man's death began the chain that produced the Mead of Poetry — the divine drink that turned anyone who drank it into a poet or scholar.

question: After the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar murdered Kvasir, they drained the wise man's blood, mixed it with honey, and brewed a magical mead. Anyone who drank from the brew would speak as a poet or learned scholar. The dwarfs poured the finished mead into three specific containers: two vats and one kettle. The mead would later be stolen by the giant Suttungr, then by Odin himself, and would become the source of all poetry in the nine worlds. What were the names of the three containers?
answer: Bodn and Son were the two vats; Odrerir was the kettle
choices: Bodn and Son were the two vats; Odrerir was the kettle
Hnitbjorg, Suttungr, and Gunnlod were the three vessels
Geirrod, Gungnir, and Gjallarhorn were the holding-vessels
Mimir, Yggdrasil, and Urd were the three sacred names
context: The names mean roughly 'Vessel,' 'Reconciliation,' and 'Stirrer-of-Inspiration.' The three-container detail is preserved in Snorri's Prose Edda. The mead would pass through many hands but the three named vessels were the original containers. Some skaldic poems refer to poetry as 'Odrerir's wave' or 'Kvasir's blood' — kennings drawn from this story.

question: Fjalar and Galar had murdered Kvasir to brew the Mead of Poetry. To cover their crime they later invited the giant Gilling to visit their hall — and rowed him out to sea to drown him, claiming an accident. When they returned home and told Gilling's wife of his death, she wept inconsolably. The dwarfs grew tired of her crying. They invited her outside to see the spot where Gilling had drowned. As she stepped through the doorway, what did they do?
answer: Dropped a millstone on her head from the roof
choices: Dropped a millstone on her head from the roof
Stabbed her with a spear hidden beside the doorpost
Pushed her into the sea where her husband had drowned
Set her dress on fire as she walked through the doorway
context: Snorri's Prose Edda preserves the gruesome detail. Gilling's son Suttungr came to demand wergild for the murders of both his parents. The dwarfs, terrified, offered him the Mead of Poetry as the price of their lives. Suttungr accepted, took the mead home, and hid it in the heart of his mountain. The mead would never have left dwarf hands without this second double-murder.

question: After Suttungr took the Mead of Poetry from the dwarfs as wergild for his parents' murder, he carried the three vessels deep into the heart of a mountain. He set his own daughter inside the mountain to guard them — sealing the rock around her so no thief could ever reach the mead. She lived alone with the brew for years, the only company being whatever the giant brought her. What was the name of the mountain, and what was the daughter's name?
answer: Hnitbjorg was the mountain; Gunnlod was the daughter
choices: Hnitbjorg was the mountain; Gunnlod was the daughter
Jotunheim was the mountain; Skadi was the daughter
Utgard was the mountain; Angrboda was the daughter
Niflheim was the mountain; Hel was the daughter
context: Hnitbjorg means roughly 'Pounding Rock' or 'Clashing Cliffs.' Gunnlod's name means 'War-Invitation' or 'Battle-Bid.' The poetic image is brutal: a young woman walled inside a mountain with the bones of a wise man's blood, waiting. Odin would come for the mead disguised as a serpent. He would seduce her in three nights to win three sips. Snorri preserves both the names and the geography.

question: Odin wanted the Mead of Poetry for the Aesir. He disguised himself as a wandering farmhand and called himself Bolverk ('Evil-Worker'). He went first to Suttungr's brother Baugi, persuaded him to help, and asked Baugi to drill a small passage through the mountain Hnitbjorg so that he could enter unseen. Baugi tried to deceive him — drilling only halfway and lying about it — but Bolverk blew sharply into the hole and the dust flew back out, exposing the lie. Baugi finally drilled all the way through. What did Bolverk transform into to slip inside the hole?
answer: A serpent
choices: A serpent
A spider
A bat
A small fish
context: The auger Baugi used was named Rati — a tool of the dwarfs. Bolverk slipped into the mountain in serpent form and Baugi tried to stab him with the auger as he went, but the serpent was already through. Snorri's Prose Edda preserves the names of all three: Bolverk (Odin's disguise), Baugi (the helper-giant), Rati (the drill). The poem Havamal also references the episode.

question: Inside the mountain Hnitbjorg, Odin (still disguised as Bolverk) seduced Suttungr's daughter Gunnlod, who had been guarding the Mead of Poetry alone for years. He spent three nights with her, and in exchange she granted him three sips of the mead. In each sip he emptied an entire vat — three sips drained Bodn, Son, and the kettle Odrerir. He fled the mountain by transforming into another shape. Suttungr discovered the theft and pursued in his own bird-shape. How did Odin escape the giant?
answer: Flew as an eagle and spat the mead into vats waiting in Asgard
choices: Flew as an eagle and spat the mead into vats waiting in Asgard
Hid the mead in a hollow tooth and walked back unrecognized
Threw the empty vats behind him as obstacles in the chase
Called down lightning that struck Suttungr from the sky
context: Suttungr also took eagle-shape and chased Odin almost to Asgard. The other Aesir set out vats on the wall to catch the mead as Odin spat it from his beak. Some drops, the Norse said, were spat backwards in the giant's terror — these became the share of bad poets. Snorri's Prose Edda preserves the bad-poet's-share detail with gentle humor. From that day, poetry in the nine worlds came from this brew.

question: Balder the Beautiful, the most beloved son of Odin and Frigg, began having dreams of his own death. His mother Frigg, terrified, set out to extract promises from every thing in creation. She traveled through the nine worlds asking each — every fire, every water, every iron, every stone, every plant, every animal, every disease — to swear never to harm her son. All swore. The gods then amused themselves at feasts by throwing spears and rocks and axes at Balder, watching the weapons bounce off harmlessly. But Loki, jealous and devious, sought out Frigg disguised as an old woman and asked her gently whether she had missed anything in her travels. What had Frigg overlooked?
answer: Mistletoe — she thought it too young and small to matter
choices: Mistletoe — she thought it too young and small to matter
The rainbow — she could not climb high enough to ask Bifrost
The wind — she did not know how to find its kingdom
Sleep — she did not think it could be a weapon
context: Mistletoe grew on the oak — a plant that lives parasitically on a tree, never touching the ground. Frigg thought it too young to swear an oath. Loki carved a dart from a mistletoe twig. Snorri's Prose Edda preserves the story in fullest detail in the Gylfaginning. The plant's Christmas associations in modern Western culture trace partly to Norse and Celtic traditions long predating the holiday's Christian overlay.

question: After learning from Frigg about the mistletoe, Loki carved a dart from a mistletoe twig. He sharpened it. He brought it to the feast where the gods were amusing themselves throwing weapons at the invulnerable Balder, watching everything bounce off. One god stood apart from the game, unable to take part. He was the blind brother of Balder, a son of Odin. Loki approached him with the dart and gentle words, offering to guide his hand. He took the blind god's fingers, placed the dart in his grip, aimed the throw. The dart flew and pierced Balder. He fell dead in the hall. What was the blind god's name?
answer: Hodr
choices: Hodr
Vidar
Vali
Heimdall
context: Hodr was Balder's twin brother in some sources, blind from birth. He had thrown the dart in innocence, not knowing what it was. The gods could not avenge Balder in his sacred hall by killing one of their own there. Later Odin fathered a son named Vali specifically to avenge Balder — Vali grew to manhood in a single day and killed Hodr. The poem Voluspa preserves this telescoped revenge.

question: After Balder fell dead from the mistletoe dart, the gods gathered to mourn. Frigg asked who would ride down to Hel and beg the queen of the dead to release her son back to the upper world. Hermod, another of Odin's sons, volunteered for the journey. Odin lent him the eight-legged horse Sleipnir for the ride. Hermod rode for nine nights through dark valleys so deep he could see nothing. He crossed the river Gjoll on the bridge that was thatched with gold, leapt over the gates of Hel itself, and rode into the hall where the dead Balder sat in a place of honor. Hermod begged Hel for his brother's return. What condition did Hel demand?
answer: Every thing in the nine worlds must weep for Balder
choices: Every thing in the nine worlds must weep for Balder
Odin himself must trade his second eye for the boon
The Aesir must surrender Mjolnir to the giants as ransom
Frigg must come down to Hel to take Balder's place
context: The image of every thing weeping is one of the most haunting in Norse mythology. Stones did weep, animals did weep, fires did weep, plants did weep. The Aesir sent messengers everywhere to ask for tears. One creature alone refused. The bridge over Gjoll was watched by a maiden named Modgud who recognized that Hermod and Sleipnir were not yet dead from their thundering crossing.

question: After Hel had set her condition for Balder's return — that every thing in the nine worlds must weep for him — the Aesir sent messengers across creation asking for tears. Every stone wept. Every animal wept. Every fire and water wept. Every tree wept. Every metal wept. But the messengers found one creature in a cave who refused. She was a giantess named Tokk who sat alone laughing dry-eyed at their plea. She said specifically what she would do with her tears. What was Tokk's line?
answer: Let Hel keep what she holds; dry tears are all I have for Balder
choices: Let Hel keep what she holds; dry tears are all I have for Balder
Balder was no kin of mine; ask his mother for water instead
I weep only for those who shared my mountain; let me alone
The dead are dead; the living should weep for themselves alone
context: The Prose Edda preserves the rhyme attributed to Tokk. The giantess was Loki in disguise. By his refusal Balder remained in Hel until after Ragnarok. The Aesir hunted Loki down and bound him for it — with the entrails of his son Vali (transformed into a wolf to kill his own brother Narvi). A serpent dripped venom on Loki's face until Ragnarok released him.

question: Odin sought the runes — the magical alphabet that contained the secret powers of speech, fate, and magic. To win them, he made a sacrifice of himself to himself. He hung from the world-tree Yggdrasil by a rope, pierced through with his own spear Gungnir. No food touched his lips, no water relieved his thirst. He hung for a specific number of nights, the wind beating the branches around him. At the breaking moment, the All-Father screamed and snatched up the runes from below — and fell from the tree. How many nights did Odin hang?
answer: Nine
choices: Nine
Three
Twelve
Seven
context: The Havamal preserves Odin's own first-person account of the ordeal: 'Wounded I hung on a wind-swept gallows for nine long nights, pierced by a spear, pledged to Odin, offered, myself to myself.' The image has been compared to crucifixion by some scholars. The runes are both an alphabet (the Elder Futhark) and magic. Odin gained the runes; the dead gained Odin as their teacher.

question: Long before Ragnarok, a stranger came to Asgard offering to build the gods a wall so strong that no giant or troll could ever breach it. He demanded payment: the sun, the moon, and the goddess Freyja in marriage. The Aesir, on Loki's advice, agreed — but only if he could finish the wall in a single winter, alone, without any help. The builder accepted the contract on condition that he could use his stallion to haul stones. The work raced ahead. The horse pulled twice the weight any horse should pull. With three days left of winter the wall was nearly complete. The gods realized he would finish in time. What was the stallion's name?
answer: Svadilfari
choices: Svadilfari
Hofvarpnir
Skinfaxi
Gullfaxi
context: To break the deal, the gods forced Loki to stop the work. Loki transformed himself into a mare and lured Svadilfari away into the woods. The work stalled. The stranger flew into a giant's rage when winter ended — revealing himself as a frost-giant in disguise. Thor crushed his skull. Months later Loki returned to Asgard leading a foal: an eight-legged colt born from his mare-form and Svadilfari. The colt was Sleipnir.

question: When Loki transformed himself into a mare to lure away the giant-builder's stallion Svadilfari, he ran into the woods in heat. The stallion broke its harness and chased the mare for days through the forest, neither caught nor lost. The wall was not finished in time and the giant-builder was killed by Thor. Months later Loki returned to Asgard leading a foal — an unusual one. It became Odin's chosen horse and the fastest steed in the nine worlds, able to gallop over sea and sky and through Hel itself. What unusual feature did the foal have?
answer: Eight legs
choices: Eight legs
Six wings
A horn of gold on its forehead
Hooves of polished bronze
context: Sleipnir's eight legs gave him impossible speed across all terrains. Loki had given birth to the foal — one of three monstrous children he had with various partners (the others being Fenrir the wolf and Jormungandr the world serpent, by the giantess Angrboda). Snorri's Prose Edda matter-of-factly records Loki as Sleipnir's mother. Snorri also said Loki could change sex at will.

question: Fenrir the wolf, son of Loki, grew so fast in Asgard that the gods became afraid. They tried to bind him with two great chains, calling each a test of his strength. Fenrir broke both easily. The gods commissioned the dwarfs to make a third fetter — Gleipnir, made from six impossible ingredients: the footfall of a cat, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird. The fetter looked like silk ribbon. Fenrir, suspicious, refused to be bound unless a god placed a hand in his mouth as pledge of good faith. One of the Aesir stepped forward and offered his right hand. Which god gave his hand?
answer: Tyr, the one-handed war-god
choices: Tyr, the one-handed war-god
Heimdall, watchman of Bifrost
Bragi, god of poets and song
Hoenir, the long-legged silent god
context: When Fenrir realized the fetter would hold, he bit Tyr's hand off at the wrist. The gods laughed except for Tyr. Snorri's Prose Edda preserves the story in the Gylfaginning. Tyr's gift of his hand made the binding possible — a small god-sacrifice that postponed Ragnarok by ages. Six of the ingredients in Gleipnir are listed as having vanished from the world afterward: that is why cats walk silently, fish do not breathe, etc.

question: The dwarfs of Svartalfheim made the fetter Gleipnir to bind the wolf Fenrir after two iron chains had failed. The fetter looked like silk ribbon — but it was forged from six impossible ingredients, each said to have vanished from the world after the dwarfs had taken them. The list survived in Snorri's Prose Edda. According to that text, what six things were used?
answer: Cat's footfall, woman's beard, mountain roots, bear sinews, fish breath, bird spittle
choices: Cat's footfall, woman's beard, mountain roots, bear sinews, fish breath, bird spittle
Dragon's tongue, giant's tooth, troll's shadow, troll's voice, dwarf hair, elf laughter
Sea foam, frost, fire, wind, lightning, and the silence of dawn
Three roots of Yggdrasil twined with three strands of Frigg's hair
context: Each ingredient was said to have ceased to exist in the world after Gleipnir was made. That is why cats now walk soundlessly, why women cannot grow beards, why mountain roots are gone, why bears' sinews lack the strength they once had, why fish do not breathe with lungs, why birds make no spittle. The mythopoetic device explains observed facts of nature as the costs of binding Fenrir.

question: After Ragnarok the world was renewed. A new green earth rose from the sea. Lif and Lifthrasir emerged from the wood Hoddmimir. Balder returned from Hel, reconciled with Hodr. A small number of the surviving Aesir gathered on the field of Ida to begin the new age. Among them were two sons of the dead thunder god, who had taken up his hammer. The brothers' names mean roughly 'Wrath' and 'Strength.' What were their names?
answer: Modi and Magni
choices: Modi and Magni
Hodr and Hermod
Vali and Vidar
Bragi and Bor
context: Magni was Thor's son with the giantess Jarnsaxa. At only three nights old, Magni had been the only being strong enough to lift Hrungnir's leg off Thor when the giant had fallen on the thunder god dying. The Vafthrudnismal in the Poetic Edda preserves the prophecy that Modi and Magni would inherit Mjolnir. Snorri's Prose Edda confirms the names and the inheritance.

question: After Ragnarok, the surviving Aesir gathered on the field of Ida. Modi and Magni inherited Mjolnir. Vidar and Vali had survived the battle alongside Hoenir. Two figures came up from the world below — Balder and his blind brother Hodr, the one who had thrown the mistletoe dart. The two embraced. They sat with the other gods on the green grass of Ida-field, talking together of things that had been. What did they find lying in the grass that had survived the burning of the world?
answer: The golden gaming pieces (chessmen) the Aesir had once owned
choices: The golden gaming pieces (chessmen) the Aesir had once owned
Mimir's severed head, still whispering wisdom from the earth
Odin's eye, returned from the bottom of Mimir's well
Bragi's harp, untouched by the flames of Surt's burning sword
context: The detail is preserved in the Voluspa. The golden gaming pieces (taflur in Old Norse) had been the Aesir's pastime before the troubles began — and they survived the burning of the world. The image is haunting: gods who had just walked through the end of time finding the small treasures of childhood, picking them up off the grass. The Norse renewal was domestic, not triumphant.

question: After the renewal of the world, the surviving Aesir gathered on the field of Ida and reigned over a new green earth. The dead who had lived virtuously rose to live in a great gold-roofed hall, the most beautiful hall ever built — said to shine brighter than the sun and to be untouched by the fire of Ragnarok. The wicked went to a different place, a hall on the corpse-shore made of woven serpents whose mouths dripped venom inside. What was the name of the beautiful hall for the blessed?
answer: Gimle
choices: Gimle
Valhalla
Bilskirnir
Sokkvabekk
context: Gimle's name means roughly 'Fire-Shelter' or 'Place Protected from Fire.' The Voluspa describes it: 'A hall I see standing, fairer than the sun, thatched with gold, at Gimle: there shall the worthy folk dwell.' The hall of the wicked was Nastrond ('Corpse-Shore'). The Christian-era poet who recorded the Voluspa may have shaped these images partly toward heaven and hell — but the Gimle motif itself is older and pre-Christian.
